and old form are attached as Annex G), so metimes amplified by correspondence bet ween the customer and the department of the Bank immediately concerned with the relevant account; (iii) where Nominees pro vides internal services for Hambros Group companies; and (iv> where Nominees, through the Bank, provides nominee servi ces for persons who are not otherwise custo mers and the relationship is therefore go verned by correspondence. It will be understood from the foregoing that, in every instance involving parties out side the Bank, the contractual obligations on the Hambros Group are undertaken by the Bank and Nominees acts entirely on the instructions and for the account of the Bank. Wc are not aware of any case in which there is any agreement between No minees and a beneficial owner. (b) Insight into Ownership by Nominees and the Bank Nominees itself requires no insight into beneficial ownership, compiling its records from and relying upon information provided to it by the Bank. Operating functions and proceedings of Nominees are the same in ca ses where the Bank itself directly or indi rectly has a beneficial interest in a company as those in which the Bank has no such in terest. So far as the Commission's enquiry rela tes to the Bank's own requirements concer ning insight in situations where shares are pledged in support of loan indebtedness, those requirements were normally limited to ensuring that the actual chargor of the sha res had duly executed a charge agreement in f avour of tne Bank. There arises in some ju risdictions a need to establish the existence of a parent/subsidiary relationship in order to verify «corporate benefit» but, in general, the Bank has no need in the case of a com pany pledging assets, to enquire in turn into the identity of that company's shareholders. Håving determined the assets over which security is required in support of a loan, the Bank is concerned to obtain a charge over those assets from their owner. Such a charge is normally obtained by an agree ment, a standard form of which is attached as Annex H. It is not uncommon, however, for these agreements to be negotiated indi vidually and their terms vary from case to case. Since charge agreements are security documents under English law it would be wrong to suggest, whatever powers of con trol might apparently be vested in the Bank, that the Bank becomes the owner oi the securities charged or (in the extreme case of a charge over 100 per cent of the shares of a company) the owner of the com pany concerned, unless and until the secu rity has been enforced.

case of a charge over 100 per cent of the shares of a company) the owner of the com pany concerned, unless and until the secu rity has been enforced.
The Bank would al ways be answerable to the chargor for hå ving acted strictly in accordance with the charge agreement and within the terms of the relevant loan. As to insight into beneficial ownership in a more general framework, single ship companies and complex corporate structures were and still are common in the shipping industry in Norway as well as in other countries and precise details of corporate ownership and inter-company relationships were therefore frequently regarded by the Bank as of little importance. Enquiries into ultimate beneficial. ownership were not pursued by the Bank in cases such as that under review where a course of dealing over a lengthy period had removed the need for such information. Each successive transac tion made the need for insight less relevant and the occasion for seeking it less approp riate. It has been suggested that the Bank should have recognised that those manage ment agreements of which it was aware were mere cloaks for the secret ownership by Mr. Hilmar Reksten of the companies concerned. Wc did recognise them as confer ring on Mr. Hilmar Reksten and/or the finn Hilmar Reksten a wide measure of control over the affairs of the relevant companies. However, there were many management ag reements, whether by provision of the bye laws or otherwise, with companies in which Mr. Hilmar Reksten was known not to have total ownership — shares in R/A Hadrian, for example, were publicly quoted — and this was a generally accepted practice. The Bank certainly did therefore regard Mr. Hil mar Reksten as managing globally very ex tensive assets. But management agreements are common in the shippingg industry and the Bank read into the known mangement agreements of Mr. Hilmar Reksten and/or the finn Hilmar Reksten no more than their terms stated. 14. In response to the invitation to elabo rate on how the Bank viewed its relations hip at the various stages under review wc would state: (a) Historically, the Bank has had close con tacts with the Norwegian authorities, repre sented both by the relevant Ministries and also by Norges Bank; it was therefore natu ral that the Bank should participate in dis cussions in 1975 on the dangers of a protrac ted shipping slump. The Bank had many loans outstanding to Norwegian shipowners to finance every type of vessel, and it was the policy of the Bank to support schemes which would prevent vessels from being the subject of forced sale.
The immediate detri ment both to the particular companies and to the Norwegian economy generally was re cognised; and the possible domino effects were such that it was not possible to say with certainty where the consequences would have stopped. When the G.I. was being established Norwegian Ministers and senior officials therefore publicly stressed that Norway would protect important Nor wegian assets, and urged that the stabilising influence, introduced by this Norwegian in itiative, should prove a catalyst for strategic planning in other countries. The Banksupported this policy and, for its own part, did nothing which might have undermined it. In theory the Bank's risk

in other countries. The Banksupported this policy and, for its own part, did nothing which might have undermined it. In theory the Bank's risk

side 265

exposure in early 1975 was relatively small — although it is recognised that the domino effects to which reference has been made would have changed the Bank's position, and also that activity in the sale and pur chase market for tankers rapidly diminis hed. Nevertheless, if action had then been taken sufficiently quickly the Bank's own position could have been protected by enf or ced sales. The Bank did not adopt such a po licy but instead granted new loans to pro vide liquidity, which were for the benefit of all creditors generally and provided the time necessary until the G.I. could become opera tional, not only to Reksten but also to other Norwegian owners. (b) Against the background of this general policy the Bank worked, together with the other Major Creditors and the Norwegian authorities, to find solutions during the Summer of 1975 to the Reksten crisis. During the many discussion it was — as stated in the Opinion (page 3) — «clear that the creditors of the group ... were fully, aware of the possibility of a «hidden» f oreign fortune.» Wc agree with this statement and the many other similar statements throug hout the Opinion. Indeed, that this should have been so was not surprising for Mr. Hil mar Reksten made no secret of the f act that during the War and afterwards he had established and maintained business con nections and interests abroad: certain na mes such as Thornhope were known to the Norwegian authorities, and wc believe that permission and/or applications for licences specifically or generally were the subject of correspondence between Mr. Hilmar Rek sten and the Norwegian authorities during the War and over the years since then. The extent is set out in some detail in the Opinion and accordingly wc do not repeat those examples. However, wc also believe that the Norwegian authorities may well have had more information on some possi bly significant matters than did the Bank. For example, it is widely rumoured that one of Mr. Hilmar Reksten's daughters at one time submitted information to the authori ties; reference to a «black book» was made in Oslo for years but no officer of the Bank has ever seen it. Copies of the Coopers & Lybrand Report were also available and it is nowhere dispu ted that all relevant parties were on notice.
Wc must therefore take particular excep tion to the view expressed in the Opinion (page 98) that the Bank gave «only a frag mentary and incomplete picture» and that «the picture which was thereby created had — seen with the eyes of the Norwegian au thorities — to weaken the assumption which the existing matters otherwise should gi ve a basis for ... Thereby it became even more difficult for the G.I. and the Norwegian authorities to base themselves on such assumptions». All the contemporary evi dence makes it clear that the Bank was fully in agreement with and assisted in the ap pointment of Coopers & Lybrand in 1975. Wc attach as Annex I a copy of a Note of a meeting with a partner of that finn, which itself referred in its Report to information håving been made freely available by the Bank, pursuant to the instructions the Bank received from Mr. Hilmar Reksten. In their Reports Coopers & Lybrand also drew attention to those areas where they had not been able to do any work, and in respect of which they felt further enquiries to be desi rable. The Bank therefore rejects this alle gation in the Opinion. It has to be added that it was said to more than one senior officer of the Bank over the years, both before and after the events of 1975, by representatives of the Norwegian authorities that they did not regard the pro per function of Hambros Bank as being a custodian of Norwegian exchange control or tax regulations. Accordingly the Bank does not believe that the view expressed in the Opinion accu rately reflects the attitude then held by the Norwegian authorities. It is also the case that representatives of the authorities on several occasions during meetings in 1975 stated that Norwegian exchange control and tax considerations were the responsibility of the Government and would be dealt with as a separate matter. (As one example, wc refer the Commission to Paragraph 5B on Page 4 of Item 12 in Annex A.) In the understan ding of the Bank this was effected through the investigation and subsequent institu tion of criminal proceedings against Mr. Hilmar Reksten, which were accompanied by extensive coverage in the media, and much of which occurred before the G.I. commitment letter was sent to the Reksten companies on 2nd November, 1976. The issues håving been separated, in 1975 the emphasis was placed on whether, and if so on what conditions and basis, a bank ruptcy might be avoided.

The issues håving been separated, in 1975 the emphasis was placed on whether, and if so on what conditions and basis, a bank ruptcy might be avoided.
That this should have been the general wish, shared by the Norwegian authorities, the Norwegian Ma jor Creditors and the Bank, was natural be cause the size and inter-relating aspects of the Reksten crisis meant that it had to be central in any national policy of stabilisa tion; and the Bank was aware of the many and fundamental shipping, industrial and credit policy considerations, the most im portant of which are set out in the Opinion and accordingly are not repeated here. Wc would only add that, delivery of newbuilding 682 (T/T «Cyprian») being imminent, it was of importance to the Akers Group in its weak financial position that delivery should be accepted and payment effected; secondly, wc understand that the capital and reserves of the Loan Institute in 1975 were such that the consequential problems of a bankruptcy could have been, if anything, more severe than even those envisaged in the Opinion. In 1976, copies of the Coopers & Lybrand Report were available to the G.I. and wc have always accepted — because of the State involvement in the G.I. — that matters known to the G.I. are to be deemed known to the authorities and vice versa. However, the question about possible assets outside Norside 266

way was not raised as being an issue rele vant to the G.I. and, as previously stated, if the size and nature of the support of the G.1., and the willingness of the Norwegian authorities generally to back schemes affec ting the Reksten companies, were funda mentally conditioned by the existence or ab sence of the widely alleged fortune, wc re main surprised that wc were never asked to communicate any knowledge that it is now suggested the Bank should have voluntee red. In fact wc do not believe the issue of the guarantees was so predicated; rather do wc strongly believe that they were issued as a matter of policy, in support of the many ob jectives, fully discussed in the Storting and elsewhere in Norway, for which the G.I. was created. For its part, the Bank throughout this pe riod cooperated in the attempt to find mu tually satisfactory solutions. To that end the Bank advanced to the Reksten companies additional loans, principally to be made available by them to the Akers Group in 1975 and 1976. The Bank also accepted the conditions imposed by the G.1., including an irrevocable forgiveness of debt and the rest rictions upon its f reedom to act implicit in a G.I. package, even though it held first mort gages on many of the Reksten vessels. Similarly, in 1978, when the G.I. renego tiated the basis of all its tanker support schemes, it would have been possible for the Bank to refuse to cooperate and to have en forced its first mortgages. The Bank urged at a meeting with the Minister of Finance on 2nd April, and as will be seen from the letters, dated 3rd April, 1978, from Mr. Char les Hambro to the Minister of Commerce and Shipping, (copies of which will be found as Items 21 and 22 in Annex A) that serious consideration shouold be given, for the rea sons stated, to the wisdom of renegotiation at that stage. Nevertheless, when the autho rities did decide to require it, the Bank again cooperated, although strong representati ons were made by all the creditors, in the Nortahk as well as in the Reksten case, that if the conditions imposed by the G.I. were too onerous creditors might not be willing to accept them. In particular, creditors found it strange that they should be expected irre vocably to write-off debt which, in the event of a return of the market, would have been to the benefit of shareholders.

they should be expected irre vocably to write-off debt which, in the event of a return of the market, would have been to the benefit of shareholders.
This repre sented a reversal of the normal principle that creditors rank before shareholders, and was also in contradiction with the G.l.'s exp ressed policy that it should be concerned with the preservation of vessels in Norwe gian ownership rather than the protection of individual shipowning companies. In short, all the creditors, and the new inves tors who had been requested by the G.I. in 1977 to consider participating in the crea tion of Nortank, had reason to negotiate as strenuously as they did and, to this end; the Bank sought meetings with Ministers and others on 26th and 27th June, 1978, to repre sent directly the general views of all creditors about the conditions then proposed, but agreement was finally reached. (c) It may be seen from many of our respon ses that the Bank viewed its valued relati onship with the Norwegian authorities prin cipally as providing an opportunity for pri vate and informal exchanges of views on matters of international importance; wc be lieve this to have been a mutual desire in view of the importance of shipping to the Norwegian economy. The ability to explore ideas before decisions were taken or actions implemented, in order that the Bank might be sensitive to the preferences of the Norwe gian Government from time to time, is so mething which was welcomed by the Bank; and wc believe has also been welcomed by the Norwegian authorities over the years. It will also be apparent that there are in stances when it is not clear whether the Bank was acting on ite own behalf or in some other capacity. It is true that in a let ter to Redernes Skibskreditforening, dated 16th February, 1976, the Bank wrote «Wc played a role in negotiating the Agreement signed on 19th September 1975, but this was not as an adviser to the Reksten companies but rather as an interested party»; however, in other instances the position was not so clear. Generally, Hambros is a merchant bank, one of the characteristics of which is that it should be ready to react to changing events and to provide its services where they are most needed from time to time. It was therefore the f act that in all shipping crises in which the Bank was significantly invol ved it consistently took initiatives. Decisi ons were always taken by the Board of the G.1., but the Bank then reacted, either by suggesting schemes or by assisting in their implementation on behalf of all parties; thus for example, together with our legal ad visers, the Bank often took a leading part in the drafting of agreements.

on behalf of all parties; thus for example, together with our legal ad visers, the Bank often took a leading part in the drafting of agreements.
Wc felt it to be correct that a leading international mer chant bank should make such direct and po sitive contributions; and wc believe that our willingness to have played such a role was generally appreciated by all the other par ties. In saying this, wc should stress that it would be wrong to draw damaging inferen ces as to why such an active role was played by the Bank in the case of the Reksten af fair: the part wc played in the Waage/Nor tank case was identical and others involved would confirm this. (d) In the event, the Bank has suffered very heavy losses and suggestions that it was able to cover these losses from outside sources are untrue. The Bank's substantial exposure to those companies of which the G.I. and the Bank were together creditors was secuered only by charges and guarantees known to the G.I. The partial repayment of the Hudson Loan, to which reference is made on page 101/2 of the Opinion, is fully explicable wi thin the provisions of the documentation available: thus the balance of that loan was stated as US$ 45,000,000 in the Coopers & Lybrand Report, and as U 5538,325,949 in

the Reksten applications to the G.1.; the provisions of paragraph 7 of the September, 1975 Agreement had in the meantime been implemented in the full knowledge of all re levant parties. The ways in which existing loans from all creiditors formed the basis of G.I. applicati ons, and the resulting detailed analysis of which mortgages were to apply to which loan and that there could be no other mort gages registered on the vessels, must conver sely have made it apparent that the Bank did not hold mortgages on those vessels as security for any loans to Palmerston, not withstanding the provisions of the licence granted by the Ministry of Commerce and Shipping on 20th June, 1973. (e) Agreement with the Trustees, March 1981 It is appropriate at this point to review the Agreement with the Trustees in view of the essential role played by the Norwegian authorities. The nature of the Proceedings against the Hambro parties has been frequently misre presented but essentially it was for the dis closure of documents. There was a strongly held view amongst counsel representing all the different defendants, that the Orders sought by the Trustees were wrongly based in English law. For the reasons given in Pa ragraph 9 of this response the Bank conside red the correct course, concistent with the best banking practice in the City of London and with propriety both to the Trustees and to the interests of existing or former custo mers, to be to permit the due process of law initiated by the Trustees to continue and to cooperate in that process. It was only in response to an initiative in February from the Ministry of Finance (wc ref er the Commission to Item 23 in Annex A) that the Bank participated in other discus sions. The Bank did not agree with certain of the points made by Mr. Erichsen, but it did respond, Mr. Perrin yisiting Mr. Erichsen to discuss the matter with him and Mr. Haug. It was suggested that, without knowing whether the Bank could cause a settlement to be effected, the Bank was willing to try to seek one if the government requested it. In the meantime the Bank did not want the London proceedings formally «stayed», being willing to have the English Courts pro nounce, after due process, whether or not the Bank should properly make the disclo sure required. These initial conversations quickly rea ched a point where the authorities wished the Trustees to participate.

make the disclo sure required. These initial conversations quickly rea ched a point where the authorities wished the Trustees to participate.
However, it was still very uncertain whether any agreement would result and accordingly the English le gal convention — since proceedings would otherwise have started shortly in the Eng lish Court — made it imperative that nego tiations between the actual parties should be on a «without prejudice» basis. It was to ensure that this was respected that a letter (a copy of which is attached as Annex J) was sent by the Bank's Solicitors to the London Solicitors of the Trustees. It will be seen that it is misleading to suggest that the Bank «whished to meet the Trustees» if that is un derstood to imply that the Bank took the initiative in seeking an agreement and that there had been no earlier initiative from the Norwegian authorities. Thereafter the documents were negotia ted with the Trustees and members of the Creditors' Committee, although at some meetings the authorities continued, in an independent role, to make their good offices available to all parties. The Bank is not privy to the motives of any of the other parties, including those of the Trustees, for wishing to proceed with an out-of-Court settlement. Among the Bank's motives, however, was the fact that the ac tion was being widely portrayed, although this was not formally correct, as being bet ween the Norwegian authorities and the Bank and wc did not wish to see this conti nue in the light of the damage it could do to that valued relationship, and to our other business in Scandinavia. Another, ana very important, consideration for the Bank was that the state of the tanker market was such that it was already apparent a renegotiation of the G.I. support arrangements for the Reksten fleet, which were due to change in January, 1982 would be necessary in any event. Accordingly, when various ideas were exp lored before the Agreement took its final form, the Bank sought to anticipate that re negotiation and to use this opportunity to reduce or eliminate problems which would anyway have to be met within months. This aspect, despite its importance, does not anywhere appear to have been recognised but it was the reason why, for example, emp hasis was placed by the Bank on the order in which proceeds, which would become avai lable for distribution by the Estate, should be applied by the creditors. This can be seen by reading the first paragraph of the letter, dated 27th March, 1981 (a copy of which is attached as Annex K), adressed to Mr. Erich sen. That proceeds should have been applied in reduction of debt ranking in priority ahead of the G.I.

«Senior Debt» figure was, and could only be, to the intent that the debt ranking ahead of the G.I. should be corre spondingly reduced, before the position of the G.I. was examined in a renegotiation. If the Bank had believed that the assessed net worth would have been significantly different, then the amount wc were willing to guarantee would also have varied. There are other misrepresentations of the nature and basis of the final Agreement. Wc attach copies of drafts and press releases as Annex L (Item 1 to 4) and invite the Com mission to compare the press release ac tually issued by the Trustees (Item 1) with their draft of that press release showing amendments proposed by the Bank (Item 2); and also to compare the draft of the accom panying press release to be issued by the Bank itself (Item 3) and that release (Item 4) as issued (but never published by the press) af ter the Norwegian authorities had sugge sted that the draft of the Bank's release would not be understood by the public. Whether or not that would have been the case the Bank believes that its suggestions for the Trustees' press release (Item 2) does, and the Trustees' press release (Item 1) does not, reflect the true nature of the settle ment; similarly, whether or not there would have been a readiness to understand it, the Bank believes Item 3 most accurately sum marizes the impact of the Agreement on the Bank.

It has been suggested that the Bank's wil lingness to engage itself in the negotiations, and the substance of the final settlement in dicated — although the actual wording of the Agreements is «2. The Trustees accept that none of the Defendants ... signifies any admission of liability ... or accept the Tru stees' rights to any remedy claimed» and «3. (iii) the Trustees in their reports ... will ... state that ... these allegations, which were denied, were not pursued» — that the Bank held assets that properly f ormed part of the Estate. The Bank did not to its knowledge hold any assets belonging to the estate of Mr. Hilmar Reksten and repeats that, at the relevant times and up to the present time, it did not and does not, to its knowledge, hold assets which should properly have been made known or delivered to the Trustees. Had any assets been held within the Ham bros Group in the nåme of Mr. Hilmar Rek sten when he died, there would have been no duty of confidentiality which would have in hibited the Bank from making immediate disclosure to the appropriate parties, whe ther his estate had been bankrupt or not. The Bank was in communication with other defendants but, in playing a leading role and agreeing the final terms, the Bank's position was that it had formulated an ag reement which it believed those defendants would accept, but which it was for them to elect whether or not to do so when asked to sign. In the event they did so, but until the day of Closing it remained a matter of some doubt to the Bank as to whether the terms of the Agreement would be fulfilled or not. The Bank does not know whether the value, which through its assistance was translated into a payment of USs4l.Bm to the Tru stees, was provided from a source of assets which, at the relevant times, would or would not have been available to Mr. Hilmar Rekcreditors. It should also be stated that, in this in stance, the Norwegian authorities did ask the Bank, both during the discussions in March, and also before Closing in May, 1981 whether it could supply further informa tion. The Bank replied that whether or not it possessed any relevant information it .was prevented by confidentiality from making disclosure; but that the Bank would ensure that the request by the authorities for an ex planation was made known to other defen dants, which wc did. The Bank has noted with concern the criticisms expressed in the Storting Debate on Ist April, 1982 which, as stated in our let ter of 25th June, the Bank refutes in the strongest terms.

Wc believe that there has been much misunderstanding, and members of the Storting may have been influenced by ill-informed press comment. Wc therefore welcome the Commission's invitation to comment an reply, and would wish to treat fully the points in the order listed by the Commission. In doing so wc act on the basis that the Commission has chosen a broadly representative selection of such criticisms and will accordingly consider that wc have answered related points made by other members of the Storting if wc restrict our comments to the examples quoted by the Commission. (a) «It is quite obvious that Hambros Bank has neglected its duty of information ... in 1976.» The Commission will already have seen from many of our answers that the Bank was not neglectful of prudent and proper

conduct; nor of a duty to disclose informa tion, even supposing such a duty to be impo sed by Norwegian law on a British bank in the circumstances under review. It is stated in the Opinion (page 107) that, in the circumstances under review, there cannot be said to have existed any need for the Bank to have given «a clear hint». The Bank was aware that the G.I. and the au thorities were on notice; that the authorities were pursuing their own investigations as a separate matter; and that such investigati ons were a separate matter; and that such investigations were to be isolated from the support of the vessels by the G.I. The telexes to which reference is made in Paragraph 5 above should also be remembered. The reasons for all parties being aware of the possibility of a foreign fortune made it necessary that the Bank should seek clarifi cation from the companies concerned, ra ther than relying upon the information which Mr. Hilmar Reksten had himself gi ven to the authorities over the years and to Cooper & Lybrand in 1975. Håving received categoric statements from the companies concerned that the assets were not to be treated, etc, and accordingly that the Bank was not authorised to release information, it would have been improper that the Bank should have given any information to third parties. (b) «The Agreement (of 1982) implied that Hambros Bank recognised that it has not behaved as it should have done in relation to the Kingdom of Norway.» Wc are particularly concerned by such statements for in the early conversations in July, 1981 with Mr. Lund, representing the G.1., when he suggested the concept that the necessary renegotiation of the G.I. agree ments should also incorporate a settlement of all outstanding questions and issues, the position of the Bank was one of considerable doubt whether a suggestion which would otherwise be commercially sensible for all parties could be countenanced by the Bank, for the very reason that the Bank's involve ment might be misinterpreted or misrepre sented. The Bank was particularly sensitive about this issue håving seen the press and other comment of the role and nature of the Bank's involvement in the Agreement with the Trustees in March 1981. This concern was repeated at many of the subsequent meetings, during which the Bank also strongly denied any allegation that it might be liable under any compensation claim to wards the G.1., the Norwegian State or any other party.

also strongly denied any allegation that it might be liable under any compensation claim to wards the G.1., the Norwegian State or any other party.
It was clear that if the Bank exploited its position as sole f irst mortgagee on nine of the twelve Reksten vessels, the Bank could have eliminated any notional security of the G.I. and the other mortgagees, their mortgages not being covered by actual values. Howe ver, the Bank did not consider that such a course would be proper, håving acted toge ther with the G.I. in support of the f leet since 1976. Additionally, such a process would obviously have been costly and timecomsuming, for it was made clear to the Bank that the Government wanted there to be negotiations between the Immediate par ties and the Bank, but that if an «economi cally and politically acceptable» compromise could not be found the Government had no choice but to submit the whole matter to ad judication by the courts. Naturally the Bank, although confident of the result, did not wish to incur the management time and irrecoverable cost of actions which would have been complicated and extremely prot racted in view of the number of the parties and issues which might have been involved; nor did the Bank wish to have the negative effects that such actions, involving the Nor wegian Government, would have had on the Bank's other business until judgment was finally obtained. Accordingly the Bank did continue with the negotiations, but when it appeared that it would be very difficult to bridge the gap betweeen the aspirations of the various par ties the Bank proposed, at a meeting in Mr. Lund's office in November, that a solution should be sought dealing solely with the dis position of the vessels, leaving all parties f ree subsequently to raise any court actions which they wished. This proposal was never followed up as Mr. Lund responded shortly af terwards, making it clear that the Govern ment was not interested in the negotiation of a proposal which did not solve all pro blems at the same time. In short, the Bank was asked to revert to what was known as the «one-track system», håving offered in all seriousness a «two-track system». The negotiations finally reached agree ment in principle but before this was an nounced, in an attempt to protect the Bank from just such innuendoes as that quoted in sub-paragraph (b) above, wc requested Mr. Lund's assistance. He therefore wrote a let ter, dated 25th November, 1981, a copy of which is attached as Annex M.
Wc under stand that he consulted the Ministry of Commerce and Shipping before signing that letter; and the Minister, in his initial an nouncement of the arrangement on Ist De cember, 1981 made it clear why certain in demnities sh6uld in the event have been in corporated. Certainly from the Bank's stance, if it was to make concessions for the reasons stated above and in accordance with the concept of a «one-track system» it wished to be certain that all outstanding issues with all creditors should indeed be dealth with at det same time. When the documents were finally agreed it will be noticed that nowhere is it sugge sted that there was any admission of liabi lity by the Bank: rather do the documents state that the agreements are intended to constitute the full and final settlement of all questions between the parties in relation to the Reksten matter and the affairs of R/A Hadrian and R/A Trajan, although the Bank did accept that the Government Dec laration must contain the stated exceptions. The Bank formally proposed, both to Nortank and to Reksten, a sale which might have been achieved on favou rable terms in January, 1981, but, when sub mitted to the G.I. for approval, the G.I. was only willing to agree to a sale if it was at a figure sufficient to cover the full pro-rata share of G.I. debt on that vessel and the price necessary to meet this requirement f rustrated the possible sale being completed. Generally the Bank would have been willing to consider a fair compromise, outside the provisions of the prevailing agreements, for the allocation of sales proceeds if any had been achieved, but the view then espressed to us by the management of the G.I. was that there was no interest in pursuing sales opportunities, despite the general sugges tion made in the Bank's letter (Annex A, Item 22, Page 2). (c) Arent M. Henriksen Many of his allegations are similar to those made by Former Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland and on those, therefore, wc comment under (d) when commenting on her allegations. However, in response to his point 4, «made a disorderly distribution among his creditors and .... Hambros Bank has known about and actively participated in this activity». Although it has frequently been asserted, in particular by the Trustees in their Provi sional Report, that assets were the property of Mr. Hilmar Reksten — or otherwise avai lable to relieve his debts (whether or not he had limited or extensive powers of control) — this is a supposition, the truth of which is not known to the Bank. The Bank has never seen proof of the assertion: if it is not correct — and it will be remembered that the sub stantial issue in the criminal proceedings in Bergen, namely whether Mr. Hilmar Rek sten had deceived the Norwegian tax autho rities by f ailing to declare prof its of the com panies the shares in or assets of which are asserted to be the assets of Mr. Hilmar Rek sten, was rejected in those proceedings — it follows that there can be no substance to the suggestion that there was a disorderly dist ribution. Wc do not consider it appropriate that the Bank should discuss the suggestoins wc have heard made as to whether the criminal court was correct in its findings, to what ex tent the same documents were available, etc.; but wc do not accept that the Agree ment with the Trustees in March 1981 itself proves the assertion, as so frequently suppo sed. If it were to be proved that Mr.
Hilmar Reksten did have a foreign fortune, which included ownership of some or all of the companies named in the Commission's questions, it does not necessarily follow that any events which occured amounted to a di sorderly distribution. And even if such a fo reign fortune existed and actions were taken by Mr. Hilmar Reksten which did amount to a disorderly distribution, it still does not fol low that this was known to or participated in by the Bank. Indeed, as the Bank acted throughout on the basis that the relevant assets were not available in a bankruptcy to relieve his debts, the Bank cannot have known or have participated in a disorderly distribution.

(d) Former Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland (i) «neglecting to inform the government about the sizeable Reksten operations out side Norway, operations which the Bank it self has participated in carrying through». The ability or propriety of the Bank disc losing information has already been discus sed in this response. There appears also to be a widespread mi sapprehension that, because the Bank did undoubtedly have a close banking relations hip with some Reksten affairs, e.g. Palmers ton where there was a management agree ment, it follows that the Bank was informed of all Mr. Hilmar Reksten's affairs and that it knew (or ought to have known) about them. This general deduction from certain specific examples is unjustified. It is now ap parent to the Bank from documents which wc first saw in the London proceedings that there was much information, which may or may not be correct but of which the Bank had no knowledge. The generalisation that the Bank was almost an «alter ego» of Mr. Hilmar Reksten himself is not correct; and, in the q\ioted instance of Palmerston, the Bank may have participated, but certain li cences were sought from the Ministry of Commerce and Shipping in 1973 and it would have been as possible for the authori ties to draw the same inferences as those which it is now said the Bank should have drawn. (ii) «Well aware that the information in the Bank's possession was not known on the Norwegian side, well aware that this infor mation according to decent business mora lity should have been made known to the Norwegian Government»; Many references will have been found throughout this response, particularly in Paragraph 14, that the Bank does not accept that the Norwegian parties were not broadly mf ormed. Wc have also stated that the Bank not only took prudent and normal care, but that, if the Bank did have any information of additional relevance, the provision of that information in the way suggested would have been contrary to accept banking prac tice and could have been the subject of grave criticism of the Bank. To suggest that the Bank should theref ore not have been involved in any agreement with the G.I. overlooks the essential pac kage nature of any solution with the G.I. It would not have been possible for the G.I.
to provide guarantees, against which liquidity could have been made available to service interest on junior-ranking mortgages, wi thout imposing restrictions on the Bank's freedom of action in respect of its first mort gages: it is hardly reasonable that the Bank should have accepted such restrictions un less it did so as part of the package. Enforce ment of the first mortgages by the Bank could have had the consequence that the vessels would be taken out of the Norwegian flag. The repercussions which the G.I. was set up to prevent would anyway have occur red, upon enforcement, and it was the Bank's policy to support objectives which were, at the time, thought to be in the best interests of Norway. (That subsequent tan ker market developments have now caused this to be questioned is, wc suggest, irreve lant; what matters is what was then com monly agreed to be in the best interests, and certainly the involyement of the G.I. with Norwegian owned rigs is now known to have had a different and positive result.) (iii) «Well aware that the lack of informa tion would impose considerable losses on the Norwegian government». In the Opinion it is accepted that the G.I. (and the State), for the reasons given, and with which wc agree, would have given gua rantees in any event. The question is there fore posed whether the Bank's alleged breach of any duty of information caused additional loss and the conclusion is drawn that it did: the Bank would strenuously deny this, and suggest that there appears here to be a misapprehension of the rules and prac tices of the G.I. A new ownership structure would, wc sug gest, only have been relevant if it had in fact entailed a harsher write-off of debt, with a corresponding reduction in the amount to be serviced with interest. Compa rison with the Waage/Nortank case, with which the Bank was also closely involved, leads us to believe that this would not have happened because the critical factors was the values assessed for the vessels by the G.I. Accordingly wc feel it necessary that wc should elaborate on this aspect: (A) Throughout the Reksten and Waage ne gotiations, the management of the G.I. made frequent reference to Schedule 4 to Storting Paper No. 17 (1975—1976) in which certain model calculations about existing and future values of vessels were made. These caulcuations clearly indicate that the basis on which the G.I. should calculate its maximum possible commitment — and the point at which it should take security — was the future expected value of the vessel, igno ring the financial position of the shipow ning company.

point at which it should take security — was the future expected value of the vessel, igno ring the financial position of the shipow ning company.
These assessed values were not necessarily the same as brokers' values. The so-called G.1.-values for the Waage fleet were «decided» in a letter from the G.1., dated 13th February, 1976, on the same day as those for the Rekstens vessels. «Based — among other things — on the said (indepen dent brokers) evaluations» the Waage/G.I. values were consistent with those for Rek sten e.g. the 1973 Akers-built 285,000 d.w.t. T/T «Radny» was assessed at N.Kr IOOm and the equivalent 1973 Akers-built T/T «Sir Charles Hambro» was also assessed at N.Kr IOOm. In this as in other regards, the nego tiations in respect of Waage were relevant to the negotiations in respect of the Reksten Group, which were principally conducted after an interim solution had been agreed for the Waage Group in March, 1976. Equally importantly, when funds avai lable under the interim solution for the Waage fleet were nearly exhausted, the G.I.

side 272

assessed new values for the fleet on 27th Ja nuary, 1977 and these values were used as the basis for all future discussions, concer ning the Waage fleet. Accordingly, the same values were used when seeking a solution within the original owning structure; and, when new investors were invited to express interest, it was on the basis that they must accept those assessed values as a minimum total for which the vessels would be trans ferred. The introduction of new investors therefore did not cause a harsher write-off of debt, and interest was serviced on the G.1.-assessed values in the new company, Nortank. Additionally the creditors reque sted, and the new investors agreed, that Nortank should accept on a contigent basis sorae additional debt in axcess of G.I. values, in respect of which interest was also serviced (at a notional rate) by drawings upon the loan guaranteed by the G.1., until after the 1978 renegotiation. (B) At the time of the renegotiation in 1978, however, the values assessed for the Nor tank vessels were higher than for the Rek sten vessels e.g. T/T «Norbright» (ex. «Radny») was assessed at N.Kr 81.3 m whe reas the T/T «Sir Charles Hambro» was as sessed at N.kr 52m. This may in part be explained by the Nor tank values being in this instance assessed later; but it was also commonly recognised at the time that, the G.I. håving invited in vestors to participate in 1977, it would not have been appropriate for the G.I. to insist upon too stringent a renegotiation since it would have been unthinkable to all parties that the company should so quickly have been forced into bankruptcy. A further sig nif icant example of this underlying f act was that, in the Reksten solution the creditors, excluding the G.1., were obligated to pay layup/operating deficits for the period 1980/81, whereas in the Nortank case these costs were exclusively for the account of the G.I. in the event of the company being unable to meet them. Whether or not new investors could have been found in 1976 for the Reksten fleet is now not possible to know, although it is a fact that it was difficult to bring to fruition initial expressions of interest for the Waage fleet in Spring, 1977. In any event, however, it is very doubtful whether the amount of the G.I. commitment would have been redu ced as the sums on which interest was paid were related to the G.I. assessed values, ir respective of the ownership of the company supported.

redu ced as the sums on which interest was paid were related to the G.I. assessed values, ir respective of the ownership of the company supported.
New capital would hypotheti cially have been injected, but it is impossible to knowhow substantial this would have been; and it is likely that much (if not all) of the benefit would have been eroded in the ways indicated above if the same principles had been adopted as were in the Nortank case. (C) It is also doubtful whether it is justi fiable to state that only debt within value should have been serviced with interest af ter the 1978 renegotiation, since, to do so, one realistically has to take not assessed values but market values, and the latter would have varied from month to month. The Pla tou values listed in Paragraph 15(b)(E) above support this. (D) The G.I. håving requested the creation of the new company R/A Trajan, an applica tion was submitted to the G.I. on Ist June, 1976. Some days later the creditors were informed that the G.I. Board had not accepted these suggested values, which they wished to see increased. It was explained the G.I. Board was afraid that if any of the old Reksten companies (e.g. R/A Julian, R/A Diocletian etc.) should become bankrupt, the transfer values could be chal lenged as being too low and thus invalidated. At the same time certain values, specifically the Hudson option vessels, were reduced so that the net effect was for the shipping as sets to be increased by N.Kr 90,679,000. (E) Certain other elements do not appear from the documents wc have received to have been taken into consideration. The G.I. was fully informed that R/A Had rian did in fact then have cash, which sub sequently the G.I. agreed might be applied as partial security for the ticket guarantee. accep ting that a new mortgage of N.Kr 48 m should be registered in favour of the credi tors on the Hadrian vessels, with priority in front of the mortgage to be registered for the G.I.
